seoDescription: Learn to run a single large language model (LLM) across multiple computers using vLLM for distributed inference. This technical demonstration details a multi-node, multi-GPU setup, explaining core concepts like tensor and pipeline parallelism. Follow a step-by-step guide to configure a head node and a worker node into a Ray cluster, serve a model like Phi-3.5, and verify its operation across all GPUs. The tutorial also covers critical environment setup, network configuration, and troubleshooting tips.

chapters.title: Understanding vLLM's Parallelism Strategies

chapters.title: Setting Up the Head and Worker Nodes
chapters.description: This chapter walks through the initial terminal setup, including connecting to the head and worker nodes via SSH and activating the necessary Conda environments.

chapters.title: Creating and Verifying the Ray Cluster
chapters.description: This section covers starting the Ray cluster on the head node, connecting the worker node, and using `ray status` to confirm that all nodes and GPUs are available.

chapters.title: Serving the Model and Sending a Test Request
chapters.description: Learn how to launch the vLLM API server with the Microsoft Phi-3.5 model across the cluster and successfully send a test prompt from a separate client machine.

chapters.title: Verifying GPU Utilization Across Both Machines
chapters.description: This chapter provides a physical tour of both computer nodes, showing the `nvidia-smi` output to confirm that all four GPUs are actively being used to serve the model.

chapters.title: Upgrading the Network with a 2.5G Switch
chapters.description: The presenter unboxes and installs a 2.5G network switch to improve the inter-node communication bandwidth between the two computers for future experiments.

chapters.title: Key Considerations and Troubleshooting Tips

chapters.title: Conclusion and Future Plans
chapters.description: Concluding the successful test, the presenter discusses the potential of this technology, future plans for experimentation with the new network switch, and some hardware upgrade challenges.

summary:
## Core Concept: Distributed Inference with vLLM

Distributed inference allows you to run a single Large Language Model (LLM) across multiple, separate computers (nodes), combining their GPU resources.

- **Benefit**: Enables running larger models that exceed the VRAM capacity of a single computer.
- **Architecture**: In this demo, a *multi-node, multi-GPU* setup is used, consisting of two computers, each with two GPUs.

## Parallelism Strategies

vLLM uses a combination of parallelism strategies for this type of setup:

- **Tensor Parallelism**: Specified with `-tp` or `tensor_parallel_size`. This defines the number of GPUs to use for model sharding *within* each individual node (computer).
- **Pipeline Parallelism**: Specified with `-pp` or `pipeline_parallel_size`. This defines the number of nodes (computers) that will work together in the cluster.

> [!TIP]
The total number of GPUs used is `tensor_parallel_size * pipeline_parallel_size`. For this video's setup, it was 2 GPUs/node * 2 nodes = 4 GPUs total.

## Setting Up the Ray Cluster

[Ray](https://www.ray.io/) is the underlying framework used by vLLM to manage the cluster of nodes.

1.  **Start the Head Node**: On the primary machine, start the Ray coordinator using `ray start --head --port=<your_port>`.
2.  **Start the Worker Node(s)**: On each additional machine, connect to the head node with `ray start --address='<head_node_ip>:<your_port>'`.
3.  **Verify Status**: On any node, run `ray status` to check if all nodes have joined and see the total available GPU resources.

## Critical Configuration & Troubleshooting

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Identical Execution Environments**: All nodes **must** have identical environments. This includes the Python version, installed packages (especially vLLM and its dependencies), and the file path to the LLM weights. Docker is the recommended way to ensure consistency. A workaround for differing paths is to create a symbolic link (`ln -s`) so the path appears identical on all machines.

- **Network Configuration**: Inter-node communication is crucial. High bandwidth (e.g., 2.5G Ethernet or faster) is beneficial.
    - You may need to specify the network interface for Ray using the `RAY_DEDICATED_NETWORK_INTERFACE` environment variable before starting Ray.
    - Find the interface name (e.g., `enp3s0` for Ethernet, `wlan1` for Wi-Fi) using a command like `ip a` on Linux.
- **Heterogeneous GPUs**:
    > [!NOTE]
    > When using a mix of GPUs with different VRAM amounts (e.g., a node with 24GB GPUs and another with 12GB GPUs), vLLM may default to using an amount of memory based on the *smallest* VRAM capacity in the cluster.
- **Finding Information**: LLMs like ChatGPT and Claude may have outdated or limited knowledge on this specific vLLM implementation. Reading official documentation and searching GitHub issues is often necessary for troubleshooting.

## Serving the Model

Once the Ray cluster is active, launch the LLM on the **head node** using the vLLM API server command:

```bash
python -m vllm.entrypoints.api_server \
    --model "microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct" \
    --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
    --pipeline-parallel-size 2 \
    --gpu-memory-utilization 0.5
```

The API endpoint will then be available on the head node's IP address, ready to receive inference requests.

So the whole idea of today's video is that these computers are actually going to be running the same LLM, however they are running it together. So all four cards among the two separate nodes are going to be working to serve the same model, which I think is something that is extremely cool in a world where you need a lot of VRAM to run some of these larger models. So instead of having to worry about shoving a bunch of cards into one motherboard and getting a Threadripper for PCIe lanes or something like that, you can actually go ahead and use multiple different systems, which allows a bit more experimentation and freedom, if you will.

Now, as this is a bit more of a technical demonstration, I think the best way to get into it is to quickly give a higher level overview of the documentation of what we're actually doing here.

Now we can see here how to decide distributed inference strategy, and if we scroll down, we see something: multi-node multi-GPU or tensor parallel plus pipeline parallel inference. Now it can get a little confusing to specifically use these terms to refer to what's going on, but essentially, if our model is too large to fit on a single node—a node being a single computer—you can use tensor parallel together with pipeline parallelism. The tensor parallel size is the number of GPUs you want to use in each node and the pipeline parallel size is the number of nodes. So essentially, to put it simply, I have two computers with two graphics cards in them each and I would like to use them all together, which in this case would lead me to the multi-node multi-GPU distributed inference setup.

## Upgrading the Network with a 2.5G Switch

All right, because I don't want the video to just be like a total whole screen recording thing, I am going to set something up that I bought specifically to allow me to experiment more with this. ## Key Considerations and Troubleshooting Tips

So in conclusion, there are just going to be a couple of specific things I want to mention just as considerations if you're going to be wanting to do this yourself. And one of those things is where right here they specifically say that it's important to make sure the execution environment is the same on all nodes, including the model path and the Python environment and things like that. And again, it is recommended to use Docker to do that, which I didn't do. I just kind of made sure that both machines had identical Conda environments and the same model path. You may notice that they do actually have slightly different names. So for this head node here where it's just `sbbs` without the one that is here, I just made a symbolic link so that as far as vLLM was concerned, they did have an identical model path.

And the only other thing I want to really touch upon here, there's two things. One is that if you are going to play with this and want to have an LLM help you or something like that, I noticed that Claude and ChatGPT do not have a lot of relevant knowledge in terms of this specific implementation of basically distributed inference with vLLM. So you may have to almost go back in time a little and actually start like reading through GitHub issues and things like that to find your answer.

And the other thing from that is that they even mention it here. So in this GitHub issue here, it is talked about how complicated network configurations can be difficult. So essentially you can see that I have these environment variables that I was running in either of the terminal windows for that specific... so for the head node I was using this, and the worker node I was using this. Basically what that means is when I type this command here, it will show me my network interfaces on this specific machine. And we can see on this one that it is connected to the rest of the network using this interface, so `enp3s0`. And we can see that. So that's why that is set to this for the environment variables that I will run on the head node. And the worker node is using Wi-Fi, so we can see here that on this interface, the `wlan1` is where it has an IP address that it can connect with the rest of the network. So that's why these are set here.

Now again, I don't actually know that like these memory limitations and things like that are things that I would have actually needed to set. This was just sort of an exploratory look into the ability to actually run models across separate computers at the same time without just having all of the cards physically connected to the same motherboard and processor and things like that.

## Conclusion and Future Plans

So I think this is really quite cool, and what actually sparked me looking at this is one of my friends and I were actually talking about running distributed LLMs and stuff like that. So I started looking into what options there were for this, and I stumbled upon this, and I think it is really cool, a bit difficult to set up, but possible as we saw here.

And of course, I'm only using Phi-3.5 Mini, which is a model that either one of these nodes could run by themselves. However, it was just kind of to get something lightweight that they could both download pretty quickly and fit and just to be able to test them. And again, just seeing the utilization in the NVIDIA control panel across both computers at the same time and then actually being able to send a request like that from a remote machine and have them in conjunction return the answer I think is really cool.

So that's going to conclude my initial testing of the distributed inference, which I think was totally awesome.
